div.p: Moving from the traditional federated design paradigm, integration of different multi-criticality functionalities onto common computing platforms is increasingly being adopted by avionics industry, driven primarily by cost and related concerns. The design of such mixed-criticality real-time systems has been recognized to be a very important but challenging problem given that safety-critical functionalities with different criticality levels must be certified correct by statutory certification authorities (CAs) at varying levels of rigorousness. Traditionally, these certification requirements are addressed by assuming the highest criticality level for all the functionalities, which is rather pessimistic, however, since certifying at the highest criticality level implies the highest degree of assurance regarding the correct behavior of all the functionalities which need to be guaranteed by over-provisioning the required resources. Therefore, it is necessary to develop new design and analysis techniques that are able to facilitate the certi fication process while efficiently utilizing the computing resources.

In this paper, we focus on scheduling and schedulability analysis problem for certifiable mixedcriticality real-time system on a uniprocessor platform. Firstly the widely-used traditional job model is generalized to mixed-criticality scenario where multiple different WCET values are specified for each job to reflect temporal constraints at all different levels of assurance. Then further investigation is conducted into an existing mixedcriticality scheduling strategy called Criticality Based Earliest Deadline First, the basic idea of which is to reserve time intervals for higher criticality jobs offline, while scheduling lower criticality jobs online at run-time using the so-called free slacks. However, the corresponding schedulability condition turns out to be incorrect. On the basis of this observation, an improved deadline-based dynamic mixed-criticality scheduling algorithm is proposed considering the design-for-certification issue, along with a revised sufficient schedulability condition deduced. And experiments conducted on randomly generated instances of jobs indicate that the proposed approach is effective and efficient.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In order to sustain the continuous growth in computing power required by avionics systems under constraints of Space, Weight and Power (SWaP), there is an increasing trend towards implementing multiple functionalities upon a shared computing platform as a means to provide more processing power per unit of volume, weight and electrical power. For example, aviation industry is contemplating Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA) architecture to achieve economic advantage by hosting multiple avionics functions on a single platform. Typically, these different functionalities do not necessarily share a common criticality level, e.g., it is more important to guarantee the correctness for flight-critical functionalities that must be performed by the aircraft in order to ensure its safe operation than for mission-critical functionalities concerning objectives like reconnaissance and surveillance. The criticality assigned to a functionality specifies the level of assurance or confidence needed regarding the correct behavior (i.e., meeting deadline) of the functionality. And some of the more safety-critical functionalities may be even subject to mandatory certification by statutory certification authorities (CAs), for example, by Federal Aviation Authority in the US or the European Aviation Safety Agency in Europe for avionics systems.

Certification is about verifying that an appropriate level of assurance in meeting the deadlines of the tasks is guaranteed. The level of assurance needed in meeting the deadlines of the tasks may be different at each criticality level. For example, in the RTCA DO-178B standard, there are five different Design Assurance Levels (DAL) for software in avionics systems, that is from DAL A to DAL E, with level A representing the potential for catastrophic failure including loss of life and/or the aircraft, with level E having no effect on safety. The design of certifiable mixed -criticality (MC) real-time systems has been recognized to be a very important but challenging problem [1], even with very simple system models as described in [2]. And techniques from conventional scheduling theory, which assumes that all the tasks in the system have the same level of criticality, cannot satisfactorily address scheduling problems arising from multiple certification requirements in MC systems. Novel scheduling theory is in need to guarantee certi fication of the system at each criticality level, while maximizing the utilization of the processor.

div.head: Related Works
div.p: The worst-case behavior of the MC real-time system during run-time must be provided to certify it as being correct, while Worst Case Execution Time (WCET) of tasks is considered mostly. Based on the observation that "the more confidence one needs in a task execution time bound, the larger and more conservative that bound tends to be in practice," the seminal work by Vestal in [3] first introduced the mixed-criticality task model, in which multiple different estimations of WCET are specified at different levels of assurance reflecting the variances in rigor adopted by the CAs. Then many researchers considered real-time scheduling techniques based on this model, with papers related to the mixedcriticality systems emerging.

Besides the MC task model, in [3] Vestal also suggested a fixed-task-priority strategy based on a specialization of Audsley's priority-assignment technique [4], for assigning priorities optimally to the tasks in the system. By showing that neither Fixed Priority (FP) nor Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling of MC tasks on uniprocessor dominates the other, Baruah and Vestal proposed a hybrid algorithm by combining the benefits of both FP and EDF policies [5]. Then improved FP scheduling algorithm and response time analysis is brought forward by Baruah et al in [6], on the basis of following implementation features: the duration of the execution time of each job is monitored at runtime and jobs of ℓ -critical tasks are dropped as soon as the system switches to (ℓ+1)-criticality behavior.

As for the more flexible fixed-job-priority algorithms, thus far, they can be generally distinguished into two categories: 1) Own Criticality Based Priority (OCBP) [2] and 2) EDF related scheduling strategy. The OCBP scheduling strategy was the first one developed for mixed-criticality jobs scheduling and an improved load-based sufficient schedulability condition of the OCBP algorithm is proposed in [7] by Li and Baruah. In [8] and [9] the OCBP scheduling strategy was extended to mixedcriticality sporadic tasks systems respectively. However, these two scheduling algorithms both have too large a run-time complexity to be implementable in practice. By adapting the traditional EDF scheduling strategy, Baruah et al. [10] proposed Earliest Deadline First with Virtual Deadline (EDF-VD) algorithm for mixed-criticality implicit-deadline sporadic task system, and also presented a utilizationbased schedulability condition for this new approach [11]. According to EDF-VD, different deadlines are used in different criticality modes, while these modified deadlines are changed on the same scale in each criticality mode. In [12] Pontus and Wang proposed a new approach similar to EDF-VD but much more flexible that allows relative deadlines of different tasks to be tuned respectively. In addition, demand-bound function (DBF) based schedulability analysis were introduced into MC scenario along with a greedy algorithm for tuning relative deadlines, on the basis of which a schedulability test was provided and proved to significantly dominate approaches from previous literature in terms of acceptance ratio. Moreover, MC scheduling on multiprocessors has also been studied recently. By applying a previously-proposed multiprocessor global scheduling algorithm called fpEDF [13] that was designed for non-MC systems, the aforementioned uniprocessor MC scheduling algorithm EDF-VD is extended to identical multiprocessor platforms in [14]. And in [15] the global FP scheduling of sporadic mixed-criticality tasks on multiprocessors is considered, along with a sufficient schedulability test based on response time analysis derived to guarantee certification at each criticality level.

In addition to the above-mentioned OCBP, another scheduling algorithm named Criticality Based Earliest Deadline First (CBEDF) is proposed in [16] to address the simpler mixed-criticality jobs 7B5-3 scheduling problem. And a load-based sufficient schedulability test for CBEDF is derived; however, it actually turns out to be incorrect as shown later in this paper. In spite of this, its basic idea still makes good sense and is worth further research.

div.head: This Research
div.p: In this paper, we address the problem of scheduling MC jobs on a uniprocessor platform by using deadline-based scheduling mechanism. And coming up with an effective scheduling strategy along with schedulability analysis that covers both the criticality and deadline aspects of MC system, while facilitating certification and efficient resource usage, is the focus of this research. To begin with, further investigation is conducted into the CBEDF scheduling strategy in [16], where a load-based schedulability condition was brought forward but actually turned out to be incorrect, that is not sufficient to determine whether an instance of MC jobs is CBEDF schedulable. In light of this observation, then an improved deadline-based dynamic MC scheduling algorithm is proposed, referred as CBEDF-I (CBEDF Improved), along with a new sufficient schedulability condition deduced. Finally experiments are conducted on randomly generated instances of jobs.

div.head: System Model
div.p: This research mainly addresses scheduling of dual-criticality task system, system with just two levels of criticality, on a preemptive uniprocessor platform. As proved in [2] that determining the feasibility of a collection of MC jobs is strongly NPhard, the simple case of dual-criticality job model is the focus of this paper. And the discrete time concept is adopted, i.e., any time value involved in the scheduling is a non-negative integer. This is based on the assumption that all events in the system happen only at clock ticks.

div.head: Problem with CBEDF Scheduling
div.p: In this section, further investigation is carried on into the CBEDF scheduling strategy [16] and existing mistakes are pointed out, with counter examples given.

div.head: CBEDF Overview
div.p: According to CBEDF, jobs having same criticality are scheduled in EDF order. And its basic idea is to reserve time intervals for HI-critical jobs offline, and then at run-time to allocate two kinds of free slacks to LO-critical jobs: One is Empty Slack after reservation while the other is Remaining Slack reclaimed from the over-provisioned capacity to HIcritical jobs.

The comparative results of different scheduling approaches are illustrated as follow in Figure 6 and Figure 7, where the percentages of instances proven to be schedulable by the five schedulability tests are presented. From Figure 6 and Figure 7, it can be seen that CBEDF-I does perform significantly better than the previous approaches EDF and OCBP, regardless of the number of jobs in an instance and the difference of deadline limit between Scene Ⅰ and Scene Ⅱ. And the performances of EDF and OCBP decrease rapidly as the number of jobs in an instance increase. It's also shown in the figures that schedulability of CBEDF-I is very similar to that of Clairvoyant, which is assumed to know the behavior of the instance beforehand.

Moreover, the performance of CBEDF is presented in Figure 6 and Figure 7, although the proposed schedulability condition is problematic. As can be seen, the difference of coverage between CBEDF and CBEDF-I is very small. To make this difference clear, their acceptance ratios are also shown in Table 2. And it is worth noting that CBEDF always dominates CBEDF-I because CBEDF may deem some instances that it cannot schedule successfully to be schedulable by error as stated by Example 1.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: This paper addresses certification-cognizant real-time scheduling problem in mixed-criticality setting, and particularly focuses on scheduling issue regarding to mixed-criticality jobs on the uniprocessor platform. Based on the observation that the previously proposed mixed-criticality dynamic algorithm CBEDF is problematic and the corresponding schedulability condition turns out to be not sufficient, an improved scheduling strategy is brought forward and a revised sufficient schedulability condition is deduced. Experimental results reveal that the proposed algorithm is effective and outperforms previous practical approaches from the literature. As future work we would like to address more general mixed-criticality systems, such as multi-criticality and sporadic task system.
